newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tax shortfall seen forcing Bonn to budget action.
newsitem.headline: Tax shortfall seen forcing Bonn to budget action.

text.p: A gloomy report due on Thursday predicting a large shortfall in German tax revenues will force Bonn to take bold steps to get its finances in order to qualify for European monetary union, analysts said.

Bonn government coalition sources said tax revenues in 1997 would be almost 20 billion marks ($11.7 billion) below expectations. Germany's finance minister had expected a tax revenue shortfall of eight billion marks.

The tax estimate report is set to cast fresh doubt over Bonn's ability to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU) and reveal the magnitude of steps needed to bring the budget under control.

Private economists said they expected Bonn to consider Draconian efforts to mop up red ink as early as Thursday evening, including clamping down on spending and risking voter anger by lifting the petrol tax.

"Germany really has to make its mind up pretty quickly what kind of EMU it wants," Darren Williams, economist at UBS in London said. "If it doesn't do something about this shortfall, it's going to be incredibly difficult for it to be choosy about its EMU partners."
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel took a bold step on Wednesday, announcing the government may sell some of its 75 percent stake in Deutsche Telekom AG earlier than expected.

Although proceeds from the sale cannot be used toward meeting Germany's deficit-to-GDP ratio as required under Maastricht single currency criteria, they can be used to cut debt-to-GDP levels, which Germany also exceeds.
Moreover, lower interest rate payments on a smaller total of German debt would enable Bonn to cut, at least by a small amount, the more closely watched deficit level.

"Now is the most uncertain time for Germany and EMU," Alison Cottrell, economist at PaineWebber in London said. "But I fully expect the political leadership to put their heads together and find a way to qualify for monetary union."
In a radio interview earlier this week, Waigel said the government would look for ways to cut spending in areas where overruns were occurring and refused to exclude a spending freeze.
Recent reports have also suggested the government was considering raising the gas tax by 10 pfennigs per litre -- a move that should increase tax revenues by around four billion marks.
Top government leaders have dismissed such reports, but economists said the ability of such a tax to quickly generate revenue would be too attractive for politicians to pass up.
"All together, Bonn may be able to improve the budget by six to seven billion marks," Gernot Nerb, economist at Salomon Brothers in Frankfurt said.
Economists said they also expected Bonn to apply pressure to individual German states to keep their spending down, adopting spending freezes if needed.

The trigger for such unpopular moves promises to be the government 1997 tax revenue estimate due on Thursday. Bonn, however, does not need to cut spending by the full expected tax shortfall -- only just enough to bring the budget overhang down to the eight billion marks already factored into the 1997 budget.
